item.title: The English Constitution
item.description:
Walter Bagehot (1826–1877) first published The English Constitution as a book in 1867. He separates the constitution into its dignified parts, such as the monarchy, which win the public’s reverence and loyalty, and its efficient parts, mainly the Cabinet and the House of Commons, which actually govern.

This copy is the 1888 London edition. It was scanned from a University of Toronto library copy and is held by the Internet Archive. The book is in the public domain.

item.title: The Accounting Game
item.description:
The Accounting Game: Basic Accounting Fresh from the Lemonade Stand teaches the language of accounting by following a child’s lemonade stand from its first sale.

The book is still under copyright, so no copy is kept here. Open Library has the catalogue record and lending options.

item.title: Ho, Canada!
item.description:
R. Rogers Smith was born in 1884 at Fort Qu’Appelle, in what is now Saskatchewan. He was a mechanical engineer and a student of international and constitutional law. His final chapter proposes a “do-it-yourself” way for an individual Canadian to assert the right to vote as a Canadian.

The 1996 edition adds the editor’s own notes in brackets. The PDF is hosted by The Myth is Canada, and the link opens their copy.

item.title: UN Convention on International Bills of Exchange and International Promissory Notes
item.description:
The United Nations General Assembly adopted this convention in 1988. It applies only to an instrument that is headed “International bill of exchange (UNCITRAL Convention)” or “International promissory note (UNCITRAL Convention)”, so the parties choose its rules by how they write the instrument.

It is a companion to the Bills of Exchange page. The link opens the official text on the UNCITRAL website.

item.title: UN Convention on the Carriage of Goods by Sea (the Hamburg Rules)
item.description:
The Hamburg Rules were adopted at Hamburg on 31 March 1978 and came into force on 1 November 1992. They govern contracts for carrying goods by sea between states, including the bill of lading, which is both the carrier’s receipt for the goods and the document of title used to transfer them.

The link opens the official text on the UNCITRAL website.

item.title: Private Enterprise Money
item.description:
Edward C. Riegel (1879–1953) argued that money is a record of value given and owed, and that traders can issue it themselves through a clearing system, without a government or a bank.

The PDF is hosted by the Community Exchange System, and the link opens their copy.

item.title: A Treatise of the System of the World
item.description:
Newton first wrote this treatise as a popular version of the third book of his Principia. It was published only after his death, in Latin and in English, in 1728. This is the English translation, in its 1731 edition.

The PDF is hosted on a Johns Hopkins University web page, and the link opens that copy.

item.title: The Law
item.description:
Frédéric Bastiat (1801–1850) wrote The Law in 1850, the year he died. He asks what law is for, and answers that it is the collective organisation of each person’s right to defend themselves, their liberty and their property. When law is turned to taking from some people for the benefit of others, he calls it legal plunder.

This edition, with a 2007 copyright, is published by the Ludwig von Mises Institute, which offers the PDF free. The link opens their copy.

item.title: Leviathan
item.description:
Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) published Leviathan in 1651. Its four parts cover human nature (“Of Man”), the making of the state by covenant (“Of Commonwealth”), a Christian commonwealth, and what he calls the “Kingdom of Darkness”.

This copy is the 1914 Everyman’s Library edition. It was scanned by the Digital Library of India from a copy in the State Central Library, Kolkata, and is held by the Internet Archive as a public-domain work. The file is about 35 MB.

item.title: The Age of Reason
item.description:
Thomas Paine (1737–1809), the author of Common Sense and Rights of Man, published The Age of Reason in parts between 1794 and 1807. Much of Part I was written in Paris as the Terror closed in, and he was imprisoned shortly after finishing it.

This copy is an ebook of the public-domain text from Wikisource.

item.title: The Gulag Archipelago, 1918–1956
item.description:
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (1918–2008) called the book “an experiment in literary investigation”. He wrote it in secret, and it was first published in Paris in 1973. Its seven parts appear in three volumes. Volume 1 (Parts I–II) covers the “prison industry”: arrest, interrogation, and the system that moved prisoners through it.

The book is still under copyright, so no copy is kept here. Open Library lends the first volume.

item.title: God Is Not Great: How Religion Poisons Everything
item.description:
Christopher Hitchens (1949–2011) was a journalist and essayist. In this book, his best-known, he takes on the major religions in turn and argues that ethics and wonder need no supernatural foundation.

The book is still under copyright, so no copy is kept here. Open Library has the catalogue record and finding options.

item.title: Foundation
item.description:
Isaac Asimov (1920–1992) wrote the Foundation stories in the 1940s, and they were gathered as Foundation in 1951, the first book of the trilogy. Seldon’s Foundation is set up to preserve knowledge and steer a thousand years of history. Each crisis it meets is settled less by force than by trade, religion and the control of technology.

The book is still under copyright, so no copy is kept here. Open Library lends it.

item.title: Two Treatises of Government
item.description:
John Locke (1632–1704) published the Two Treatises anonymously in 1689. The first tears down Sir Robert Filmer’s claim that kings inherit Adam’s authority. The second asks where lawful power comes from and finds it in the consent of the governed. Its chapter “Of Property” argues that a man owns what he mixes his labour with, and that government exists to protect that property.

This copy is the public-domain text of volume V of the 1823 Works of John Locke, prepared by Rod Hay for the McMaster University Archive of the History of Economic Thought (216 pages).
